title: Paraguay's Senate moves to try President Peña after he quits over Ueno bank collapse
dek: Congress has not accepted Santiago Peña's resignation after a digital bank serving most of the country's adults failed; deputies voted 78-0 to impeach him and prosecutors have opened three investigations.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Paraguay's Senate on Friday pressed ahead with impeachment proceedings against President Santiago Peña, a day after he announced his resignation over the collapse of Ueno, a digital bank that held the savings of millions of Paraguayans and hundreds of millions of dollars in public money. Congress has not accepted the resignation, leaving the South American country's leadership in limbo.

The lower house voted 78-0 on Thursday to impeach Mr Peña minutes after he released a recorded video announcing that he would step down. The Senate convened an extraordinary session on Friday to take up the charges, and prosecutors have opened criminal investigations that include allegations involving the president. Vice President Pedro Alliana, who would serve out the term if Mr Peña goes, had not been sworn in by Friday, according to reports.

## What happened

The crisis moved fast. On Monday, 2 November, regulators reviewing Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending and expenses wrongly counted as assets, according to reports. Once the books were corrected, the bank's capital fell to less than half the legal minimum.

On Tuesday the central bank took control of Ueno, saying it would move customer accounts and any valuable assets to other banks before liquidating what was left. The bank's app, cards and transfers stopped working and its branches closed. The same day the central bank's president, Carlos Carvallo, resigned. Mr Carvallo had previously headed Financiera Ueno, the finance company from which the bank grew, and had been appointed by Mr Peña.

On Wednesday Congress passed a law requiring a state deposit guarantee fund to repay customers within five business days, starting with small accounts, and an interim central bank chief, Pedro Acosta Bernal, was named. "The banking system is sound," he said, according to reports. Thousands of retirees, depositors, students and workers marched on Congress in Asunción.

On Thursday Mr Peña announced his resignation. He said he was acting with "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind", and apologised "if I have failed them at any point", according to reports. He did not accept responsibility for the bank's collapse.

## Resignation and impeachment

Minutes later, all 78 deputies present in the lower house voted to impeach him and send the case to the Senate. Both main factions of Mr Peña's own Colorado Party backed the move after former President Horacio Cartes, the party's leader and Mr Peña's political mentor, withdrew his support. "We will not side with the theft of public, private and pension funds," Mr Cartes wrote on social media, according to reports.

A joint session of Congress to receive the resignation lost its quorum when Colorado lawmakers walked out, so it was not formally accepted, according to reports. Lawmakers acting as prosecutors filed the charges on Thursday evening. They accuse Mr Peña of conflicts of interest, manipulating regulatory oversight, diverting pension funds and an institutional cover-up involving the central bank, reports said. Mr Peña held a stake in a company linked to Ueno's parent group, Grupo Vázquez, until 2025; he says he sold it.

On Friday the Senate opened its session. Mr Peña's lawyers asked for 72 hours to prepare his defence; one report said the Senate rejected the request. Conviction needs a two-thirds vote in the Senate and would strip Mr Peña of the lifetime Senate seat that former presidents receive, along with its legal immunity. Opposition lawmakers had argued that a resignation alone would leave him eligible for that seat.

The lower house separately shelved an impeachment request against Mr Alliana on Thursday, by 48 votes to 30, according to reports. Opposition deputies had accused him of using his role as the government's link to Congress to block questions about Ueno and the central bank.

## The bank and the money

Ueno, a rebranded finance company that won a banking licence in 2023, said it served nearly 3 million people, more than 60% of Paraguay's adults, according to reports. Paraguay has about 6.5 million people.

- Public money: Ueno reported roughly $800 million in public deposits last month, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of hydroelectric dams; another report put public funds at about $850 million
- Guarantee: the deposit fund covers balances up to about $36,000 to $38,000 (reports differ), which the central bank says covers the full balance of about 97% of customers
- Accounts moved: about 280,000 people who banked only with Ueno have been given accounts at other banks, officials said
- Jobs: the Labour Ministry estimates about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs are affected

Some customers began recovering money on Thursday night, according to reports. Holders of larger balances, including the public institutions, face an uncertain wait.

## The criminal cases

Attorney General Emiliano Rolón Fernández ordered three criminal investigations, covering oversight of the bank, the handling of its failure, and the placing of public funds in it, including allegations involving Mr Peña and current and former officials, according to reports. No charges against Mr Peña had been reported by Friday. Mr Peña has said he will cooperate with investigators.

Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offences including breach of trust and attempted fraud. A judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank president Juan Manuel Gustale, held in jail pending trial and two others placed under house arrest, reports said. None of the accused has been convicted.

## What they are saying

Protesters outside Congress urged lawmakers not to let Mr Peña resign before he could be tried. "Let the impeachment process take place and let him lose his immunity," one protester told reporters. Ueno employees whose wages are trapped in the failed bank protested outside the Labour Ministry.

Mr Peña, 47, a former IMF economist, wrote on social media that "whatever the outcome of this process, I will act with responsibility and respect for the Constitution", according to reports.

## Why it matters

Operators of the hydroelectric dams that Paraguay shares with its neighbours had money in Ueno, and Brazil's immediate concern is avoiding social unrest and a wider banking crisis, one report said, citing a Brazilian government source. Mr Peña has been seen as one of the Latin American leaders most closely aligned with US President Donald Trump.

For regulators elsewhere, including India's, the episode is a case study of a fast-growing digital lender that signed up most of a country's adults while lending to its owners' companies. Ueno's bonds are separate from Paraguay's sovereign debt, analysts said.

## What happens next

The Senate must decide whether to proceed to a full trial or let the resignation close the matter, and whether to grant Mr Peña more time for his defence. If he is removed or his resignation is accepted, Mr Alliana, 52, a Colorado Party politician and Mr Peña's 2023 running mate, would serve until the term ends in August 2028, and Congress would have to choose a new vice-president. Depositors are watching whether the guarantee fund pays out on time.
